stage_description: The senior stage begins around 3–4 years, within a typical 5–10 year lifespan. Activity and metabolism gradually slow, ferrets sleep more, and some muscle may be lost. This is the age when adrenal disease and insulinoma become notably common in ferrets, so early detection through routine screening becomes the priority.
nutrition: Continue a high-quality diet rich in animal protein and fat, offered in an easily eaten form. Watch that intake stays adequate, monitor weight closely, and keep water easy to reach. If a health condition is present, follow any diet adjustments your vet recommends.
activity: Keep up gentle daily play and enrichment to preserve muscle and mental sharpness, while allowing for more frequent naps. Provide soft bedding, warmth, and low ramps or easy-access litter boxes so an aging ferret can move around comfortably.
veterinary_check_frequency: Move to wellness exams every 6 months, with a weight check, physical exam, and bloodwork that includes blood glucose, to catch adrenal disease and insulinoma early. Keep vaccinations current with an exotics or ferret vet.
dental_care: Aging teeth accumulate more tartar, and gum disease or worn and fractured canines become more likely. Keep brushing at home and include a dental assessment at each veterinary visit.
warning_signs: See an exotics vet promptly for symmetrical hair loss (often starting at the tail), a swollen vulva in a spayed female, hind-limb weakness, staring or drooling, lethargy, weight loss, or a marked change in appetite — common signs of the diseases seen at this age.
